\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The tree}
Let $\Z^{3}$ carry the Lorentz form of signature $(2,1)$,
\[
Q(a,b,c)=a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2},\qquad Q_{L}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1),
\]
and call $v$ \emph{on the cone} if $Q(v)=0$. Define
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&2\\2&-1&2\\2&-2&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&2\\2&1&2\\2&2&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
C=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2&2\\-2&1&2\\-2&2&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each satisfies $M^{\mathsf T}Q_{L}M=Q_{L}$, hence maps Pythagorean triples to Pythagorean triples.
Write $\Gen=\{A,B,C\}$ and let $g\cdot r$ denote the result of applying a finite word
$g\in\Gen^{*}$ to the root $r=(3,4,5)$. By the Barning--Berggren--Hall theorem, $g\mapsto g\cdot r$
is a bijection from $\Gen^{*}$ onto the primitive Pythagorean triples with even second leg. In
particular the tree is free: distinct addresses give distinct triples, and every node has exactly
three children. Its boundary is
\[
\partial\mathcal{T}=\Gen^{\N}=\{A,B,C\}^{\N},
\]
a Cantor set with the Bernoulli measure assigning mass $3^{-n}$ to each cylinder of length $n$.

\subsection{The coincidences and the conjecture}
Four facts conspire. (i) $\det(XI-B)=(X+1)(X^{2}-6X+1)$, so $B$ has eigenvalues $-1$ and
$3\pm2\sqrt2$. (ii) $3+2\sqrt2=(1+\sqrt2)^{2}$ is the square of the fundamental unit of
$\Q(\sqrt2)$. (iii) The tree is $(q+1)$-regular with $q=2$, and $2$ ramifies in $\Q(\sqrt2)$ as
$(\sqrt2)^{2}$ with residue field of size $2$. (iv) The hypotenuses along the all-$B$ branch obey
$c_{n+2}=6c_{n+1}-c_{n}$, whose reciprocal characteristic polynomial factors as
$1-6x+x^{2}=(1-(3+2\sqrt2)x)(1-(3-2\sqrt2)x)$, precisely the shape of an unramified local Euler
factor with Satake parameters $3\pm2\sqrt2$.

Since boundaries of $(q+1)$-regular trees are the standard models of local Hecke theory, one is
tempted to conjecture that the Berggren boundary supports Hilbert modular forms for $\Q(\sqrt2)$
with Hecke eigenvalues $3\pm2\sqrt2$. Sections \ref{sec:trace}, \ref{sec:hecke} and
\ref{sec:locus} refute this in three independent ways; Sections \ref{sec:silver},
\ref{sec:hyperbolic} and \ref{sec:trichotomy} establish the positive structure that replaces it.

\section{The silver coordinate}\label{sec:silver}

\begin{definition}
For $v=(a,b,c)\in\Z^{3}$ set
\[
\zeta(v)=(a+b)+c\sqrt2\in\Z[\sqrt2],\qquad \zeta^{-}(v)=(a-b)+c\sqrt2 .
\]
Write $\lambda=3+2\sqrt2$ and $\bar\lambda=3-2\sqrt2$, so $\lambda\bar\lambda=1$,
$\lambda+\bar\lambda=6$ and $\lambda=(1+\sqrt2)^{2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Intertwining]\label{thm:intertwine}
For all $v=(a,b,c)$,
\[
\zeta(Bv)=\lambda\,\zeta(v),\qquad
\zeta(Av)=\lambda\,\zeta^{-}(v),\qquad
\zeta(Cv)=\lambda\bigl((b-a)+c\sqrt2\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first two coordinates of $Bv$ sum to $3(a+b)+4c$, and its third coordinate is $2(a+b)+3c$;
hence
$\zeta(Bv)=(3(a+b)+4c)+(2(a+b)+3c)\sqrt2=(3+2\sqrt2)((a+b)+c\sqrt2)$, using $\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=2$.
The other two cases are the same computation with $a-b$ resp.\ $b-a$ in place of $a+b$.
\end{proof}

Thus exactly one letter acts as a $\Z[\sqrt2]$-scalar on its own coordinate; the other two act
after a leg swap. This asymmetry drives everything below.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{spine} is $s_{0}=(3,4,5)$, $s_{n+1}=Bs_{n}$: explicitly
$(3,4,5)$, $(21,20,29)$, $(119,120,169)$, $(697,696,985)$, $(4059,4060,5741),\dots$
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Spine is the unit orbit]\label{thm:spine}
$\zeta(s_{n})=(1+\sqrt2)^{2n+3}$ for all $n\ge0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\zeta(3,4,5)=7+5\sqrt2=(1+\sqrt2)^{3}$, and Theorem \ref{thm:intertwine} multiplies by
$\lambda=(1+\sqrt2)^{2}$ at each step.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Negative Pell]\label{cor:pell}
Writing $s_{n}=(a_{n},b_{n},c_{n})$ we have $(a_{n}+b_{n})^{2}-2c_{n}^{2}=-1$, equivalently
$c_{n}^{2}-2a_{n}b_{n}=1$; in particular every $\zeta(s_{n})$ is a unit of $\Z[\sqrt2]$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The norm $N(x+y\sqrt2)=x^{2}-2y^{2}$ is multiplicative and $N(1+\sqrt2)=-1$, so
$N(\zeta(s_{n}))=(-1)^{2n+3}=-1$. The second form uses $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact rate of approach]\label{thm:rate}
For all $n$,
\[
\left(\frac{a_{n}+b_{n}}{c_{n}}\right)^{2}=2-\frac{1}{c_{n}^{2}},
\]
so $(a_{n}+b_{n})/c_{n}\to\sqrt2$ with error $O(c_{n}^{-2})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Divide $(a_{n}+b_{n})^{2}=2c_{n}^{2}-1$ by $c_{n}^{2}$; positivity of the coordinates and
$3^{n}\le c_{n}$ give convergence to the positive root.
\end{proof}

\section{The hyperbolic generator}\label{sec:hyperbolic}

\begin{theorem}[Eigen-decomposition over $\Z[\sqrt2]$]\label{thm:eigen}
Extending $B$ to $\Z[\sqrt2]^{3}$,
\[
B(1,1,\sqrt2)=\lambda(1,1,\sqrt2),\quad
B(1,1,-\sqrt2)=\bar\lambda(1,1,-\sqrt2),\quad
B(1,-1,0)=-(1,-1,0),
\]
and $Q(1,1,\pm\sqrt2)=0$, so the two hyperbolic eigenvectors are light-like. Moreover
$\det(XI-B)=(X+1)(X^{2}-6X+1)$, and $X^{2}-6X+1$ is the minimal polynomial of $\lambda$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each eigen-relation is a direct matrix--vector computation in $\Z[\sqrt2]$; for instance the third
coordinate of $B(1,1,\sqrt2)$ is $2+2+3\sqrt2=4+3\sqrt2=(3+2\sqrt2)\sqrt2$. The characteristic
polynomial factors because $\tr B=5$ and $\det B=-1$.
\end{proof}

Geometrically $B$ is a hyperbolic isometry with axis joining the ideal points
$[1:1:\sqrt2]$ and $[1:1:-\sqrt2]$ and translation length $\log\lambda$.

\begin{remark}[Spin representation]
In Euclid coordinates $(a,b,c)=(m^{2}-n^{2},2mn,m^{2}+n^{2})$ the generators act on $(m,n)$ by
\[
A\leftrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
B\leftrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
C\leftrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
all in $\mathrm{GL}(2,\Z)$. The spin matrix of $B$ has characteristic polynomial $X^{2}-2X-1$ and
eigenvalues $1\pm\sqrt2$: the three-dimensional eigenvalue is the square of the two-dimensional
one, so the fundamental unit is a spinor eigenvalue of the tree.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Pell recursion and Binet formula]\label{thm:binet}
$c_{n+2}=6c_{n+1}-c_{n}$ with $c_{0}=5$, $c_{1}=29$, and
\[
c_{n}=\alpha\lambda^{n}+\beta\bar\lambda^{\,n},\qquad
\alpha=\frac{7+5\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2},\qquad \beta=\frac{7-5\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}.
\]
Moreover $-\tfrac12<\beta<0$ and $0<\bar\lambda<\tfrac15$, so $c_{n}$ is the nearest integer to
$\alpha\lambda^{n}$, and $c_{n+1}/c_{n}\to\lambda$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $p_{n}=a_{n}+b_{n}$ one has $p_{n+1}=3p_{n}+4c_{n}$ and $c_{n+1}=2p_{n}+3c_{n}$; eliminating
$p$ gives the recursion. Since $\lambda,\bar\lambda$ are the roots of $X^{2}=6X-1$, the closed form
holds once the initial values match:
$\alpha-\beta=\frac{10\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}=5=c_{0}$ and $\alpha\lambda-\beta\bar\lambda=29=c_{1}$.
Numerically $\beta\approx-0.0251$, so $|\beta\bar\lambda^{n}|<\tfrac12$ for all $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Euler-factor shape]\label{thm:euler}
$(1-\lambda x)(1-\bar\lambda x)=1-6x+x^{2}$.
\end{theorem}

This has exactly the shape of an unramified local Euler factor with Satake parameters
$\lambda,\bar\lambda$. Section \ref{sec:satake} shows the resemblance is superficial.

\section{Obstruction I: the invariant trace field is $\Q$}\label{sec:trace}

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the monoid generated by $A,B,C$ in $\mathrm{GL}(3,\Z)$ and
$\mathcal{M}_{\R}$ its image in $\mathrm{GL}(3,\R)$.

\begin{proposition}
$\mathcal{M}\subseteq \mathrm{O}(2,1;\Z)=\{M\in\mathrm{GL}(3,\Z):M^{\mathsf T}Q_{L}M=Q_{L}\}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Integral traces]\label{thm:tracesint}
Every $M\in\mathcal{M}$ has $\tr M\in\Z$; in particular $\tr M$ is never irrational. Concretely
$\tr A=\tr C=3$ and $\tr B=5$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Matrices with integer entries form a ring containing the generators, hence containing
$\mathcal{M}$; the trace of such a matrix is a sum of integers.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No Hilbert modular element conjugates in]\label{thm:noconj}
Let $H=\begin{pmatrix}1+\sqrt2&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\Z[\sqrt2])$, so
$\tr H=1+\sqrt2$ and its three-dimensional adjoint has trace $(\tr H)^{2}-1=2+2\sqrt2$; both are
irrational. If $M\in\mathrm{GL}(3,\R)$ has $\tr M=2+2\sqrt2$, then $gMg^{-1}\notin\mathcal{M}_{\R}$
for every $g\in\mathrm{GL}(3,\R)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Trace is a conjugation invariant, so $\tr(gMg^{-1})=2+2\sqrt2$ is irrational, contradicting
Theorem \ref{thm:tracesint}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The invariant trace field of the Berggren tree is $\Q$, not $\Q(\sqrt2)$: no conjugate of the
Berggren monoid contains the adjoint of $H$, so the tree does not generate a Hilbert modular group.
Its natural home is $\mathrm{O}(2,1;\Z)$, whose spin form is $\mathrm{GL}(2,\Z)$.
\end{corollary}

Hyperbolic elements of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\Z)$ routinely have quadratic irrational eigenvalues; the
eigenvalue field of one element says nothing about the field of definition of the group.

\section{Obstruction II: the boundary Hecke spectrum is $\{0,3\}$}\label{sec:hecke}

\begin{definition}
The boundary is $\Bdry=\Gen^{\N}$. For $x\in\Gen$, $x\frown w$ prepends $x$ to $w$, and
$\sigma w=w(\cdot+1)$ is the one-sided shift, so $\sigma(x\frown w)=w$ and $w(0)\frown\sigma w=w$.
An \emph{observable} is a function $f:\Bdry\to\R$; the space of these is $\Obs$. Define
\[
(Tf)(w)=\sum_{x\in\Gen}f(x\frown w)\quad\text{(Hecke/transfer operator)},\qquad
(Uf)(w)=f(\sigma w)\quad\text{(shift operator)} .
\]
\end{definition}

$T$ is the local Hecke operator of a $(q+1)$-regular tree with $q=2$; $U$ is the composition
operator of the shift. No topology or measure is required for what follows.

\begin{theorem}[Hecke relations]\label{thm:relations}
$TU=3\,\mathrm{id}$, and consequently $H:=UT$ satisfies $H^{2}=3H$; hence $E=\tfrac13H$ is
idempotent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$(T(Uf))(w)=\sum_{x}f(\sigma(x\frown w))=\sum_{x}f(w)=3f(w)$ since $|\Gen|=3$. Then
$H^{2}=U(TU)T=3UT=3H$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical splitting]\label{thm:splitting}
$\Obs=\image E\oplus\ker E$, with
\[
\image E=\{f:Hf=3f\}=\image U,\qquad \ker E=\{f:Hf=0\}=\ker T .
\]
Every observable is uniquely $f=g+h$ with $Hg=3g$ and $Hh=0$, namely $g=\tfrac13Hf$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The splitting is the standard decomposition attached to an idempotent. If $f=Ug$ then
$Hf=UTUg=3Ug=3f$; conversely $Hf=3f$ gives $f=U(\tfrac13Tf)$. If $Hf=0$, evaluating $UTf$ at
$A\frown w$ gives $(Tf)(w)=0$; the converse is immediate. Uniqueness follows by applying $H$ to
$g_{1}+h_{1}=g_{2}+h_{2}$, which yields $3g_{1}=3g_{2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
If $f\neq0$ and $Hf=\mu f$ then $\mu\in\{0,3\}$, and both values occur. Hence the eigenvalue
spectrum of the boundary Hecke operator is exactly $\{0,3\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Applying $H$ gives $\mu^{2}f=H^{2}f=3Hf=3\mu f$, so $\mu(\mu-3)=0$. The constant observable
satisfies $H\mathbf1=3\mathbf1$ (the trivial or Eisenstein eigenform, with the degree eigenvalue
$q+1=3$); the first-letter observable $f(w)=\varepsilon(w_{0})$ with
$\varepsilon(A)=1,\varepsilon(B)=-1,\varepsilon(C)=0$ has $Tf=0$, hence $Hf=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Falsification]\label{cor:falsif}
For every $f\neq0$ we have $Hf\neq(3+2\sqrt2)f$ and $Hf\neq(3-2\sqrt2)f$: the silver units are not
Hecke eigenvalues of the boundary.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem \ref{thm:dichotomy} an eigenvalue is $0$ or $3$; but $1<\sqrt2<\tfrac32$ gives
$3+2\sqrt2>5$ and $0<3-2\sqrt2<1$.
\end{proof}

The boundary therefore carries a genuine but \emph{degenerate} Hecke algebra: a rank-one Hecke pair
whose only eigenvalues are $0$ and the trivial degree eigenvalue $q+1$. There is no family of
Hecke eigenforms with varying eigenvalues, hence no automorphic spectrum to speak of.

\section{Obstruction III: the $\Q(\sqrt2)$-locus is one geodesic}\label{sec:locus}

\begin{theorem}[Norm identity]\label{thm:norm}
If $v=(a,b,c)$ is on the cone then $N(\zeta(v))=(a+b)^{2}-2c^{2}=-(a-b)^{2}$. Hence $\zeta(v)$ is a
unit of $\Z[\sqrt2]$ if and only if $|a-b|=1$, if and only if $(a+b)^{2}-2c^{2}=-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$(a+b)^{2}-2c^{2}=a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}-2(a^{2}+b^{2})=-(a-b)^{2}$, and an element of $\Z[\sqrt2]$ is a
unit exactly when its norm is $\pm1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Leg-difference dynamics]\label{lem:legdiff}
With $d(v)=a-b$ and $p(v)=a+b$: $d(Av)=-p(v)$, $d(Bv)=-d(v)$, $d(Cv)=p(v)$.
\end{lemma}

Every node is \emph{admissible}: $0<a$, $0<b$, $a<c$, $b<c$ (preserved by all three generators,
true at the root), so $p(v)\ge7$ everywhere. Hence $A$ and $C$ push the leg difference to at least
$7$ and, since $p$ only grows, the unit property never returns.

\begin{theorem}[Unit locus]\label{thm:unitlocus}
For a finite address $g$, the node $g\cdot r$ has unit silver coordinate if and only if every letter
of $g$ is $B$; equivalently $g\cdot r=s_{|g|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $|g|$ using Theorem \ref{thm:norm} and Lemma \ref{lem:legdiff}: $B$ preserves $|d|$,
while $A$ and $C$ replace it by $p\ge7$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Boundary locus is a point]\label{thm:boundarylocus}
\[
\bigl\{w\in\Bdry:\ \zeta\bigl((w_{0}\cdots w_{n-1})\cdot r\bigr)\text{ is a unit for all }n\bigr\}
=\{BBB\cdots\}.
\]
In particular the $\Q(\sqrt2)$-locus of the boundary has Hausdorff dimension $0$ inside a Cantor
set of full dimension, and Bernoulli measure zero.
\end{theorem}

Automorphic forms on a tree boundary are supported on the whole boundary; here the arithmetic of
$\Q(\sqrt2)$ is confined to a single geodesic ray and its endpoint.

\section{The mechanism: spectral trichotomy of the alphabet}\label{sec:trichotomy}

\begin{theorem}[Parabolic letters]\label{thm:parabolic}
$\det(XI-A)=\det(XI-C)=(X-1)^{3}$, and $(A-I)^{3}=0\neq(A-I)^{2}$, $(C-I)^{3}=0\neq(C-I)^{2}$: the
letters $A$ and $C$ are unipotent with a single maximal Jordan block, i.e.\ parabolic isometries.
Moreover $A$ fixes the rational light-like vector $(0,1,1)$ and $C$ fixes $(1,0,1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No rational ideal point for $B$]\label{thm:norational}
There is no nonzero $v\in\Q^{3}$ with $Q(v)=0$ and $Bv=\mu v$ for some $\mu\in\Q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem \ref{thm:eigen} such a $v$ must be proportional to $(1,1,\pm\sqrt2)$, which would force
$2y^{2}=x^{2}$ with rational $x,y$, $y\neq0$, contradicting the irrationality of $\sqrt2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Growth signatures]\label{thm:growth}
$A^{n}r=(2n+3,\,2n^{2}+6n+4,\,2n^{2}+6n+5)$ and $C^{n}r=(4n^{2}+8n+3,\,4n+4,\,4n^{2}+8n+5)$: the
parabolic branches grow quadratically. The hyperbolic branch grows exponentially,
$c_{n}\sim\alpha(3+2\sqrt2)^{n}$ by Theorem \ref{thm:binet}.
\end{theorem}

So the alphabet contains two parabolics fixing rational cusps and one hyperbolic with quadratic
irrational axis. Real quadratic irrationalities in a $\Q$-arithmetic group appear exactly as the
fixed points and multipliers of its hyperbolic elements --- which is precisely what happens here.

\section{Temperedness and Satake normalization}\label{sec:satake}

\begin{theorem}[Ramanujan bound violated]\label{thm:tempered}
The prime $(\sqrt2)$ of $\Z[\sqrt2]$ is ramified above $2$ with residue field of cardinality $q=2$,
so the temperedness bound for a local Hecke eigenvalue there is $|\mu|\le2\sqrt q=2\sqrt2$. But
$2\sqrt2<3$ and $2\sqrt2<3+2\sqrt2$, so neither the actual boundary eigenvalue $3$ nor the
hypothetical eigenvalue $3+2\sqrt2$ is tempered.
\end{theorem}

The failure at $\mu=3$ is expected: $q+1$ is the trivial eigenvalue of any $(q+1)$-regular tree.
The point is that the tree has \emph{no other} nonzero eigenvalue.

\begin{theorem}[Not a Satake pair]\label{thm:satake}
$(3+2\sqrt2)(3-2\sqrt2)=9-8=1\neq2=q$.
\end{theorem}

An unramified representation of $\mathrm{GL}(2)$ with trivial central character over a local field
with residue cardinality $q$ has Satake parameters of product $q$ in the classical normalization
(or product $1$ with both of absolute value $1$ in the unitary normalization). The Berggren pair has
product $1$ because $3\pm2\sqrt2$ are conjugate units of norm one, while $|3+2\sqrt2|\approx5.83$
is far from the unit circle. The polynomial $1-6x+x^{2}$ of Theorem \ref{thm:euler} is therefore
the Euler factor of a real quadratic unit, not of a Hilbert modular form.

\section{Algorithms and numerics}

Four exact computations underpin the results.

\emph{Tree traversal.} Breadth-first application of $A,B,C$ to $(3,4,5)$, carrying for each node its
address, triple, silver coordinate as an exact pair $(x,y)$ with $\zeta=x+y\sqrt2$, and its norm
$x^{2}-2y^{2}$. Cost $O(3^{n})$ to depth $n$ with $O(1)$ big-integer operations per node. This
verifies $N(\zeta)=-(a-b)^{2}$ and Theorem \ref{thm:unitlocus}.

\emph{Spine arithmetic.} Iterate $s_{n+1}=Bs_{n}$ and multiply in $\Z[\sqrt2]$ via
$(x_{1},y_{1})(x_{2},y_{2})=(x_{1}x_{2}+2y_{1}y_{2},\,x_{1}y_{2}+x_{2}y_{1})$ to confirm
$\zeta(s_{n})=(1+\sqrt2)^{2n+3}$ and $(a_{n}+b_{n})^{2}-2c_{n}^{2}=-1$. Cost $O(n)$.

\emph{Binet check.} Compute $c_{n}$ by the recursion and independently as
$\mathrm{round}(\alpha\lambda^{n})$ in high precision; the two agree and
$|c_{n}-\alpha\lambda^{n}|<\tfrac12$.

\emph{Finite-depth Hecke spectrum.} Observables depending on the first $k$ letters form
$\R^{3^{k}}$, on which $H=UT$ is an explicit $3^{k}\times3^{k}$ matrix with eigenvalue $3$ of
multiplicity $3^{k-1}$ and eigenvalue $0$ of multiplicity $3^{k}-3^{k-1}$ --- and nothing else, for
every $k$, in agreement with Theorem \ref{thm:dichotomy}.

\section{Discussion and future directions}

\subsection{What is true} The silver coordinate intertwines the hyperbolic generator with
multiplication by $(1+\sqrt2)^{2}$; the all-$B$ spine is the orbit of the root under the unit group,
consists exactly of the almost-isoceles triples, and solves the negative Pell equation; the
eigen-data of $B$ over $\Z[\sqrt2]$ identify the ideal endpoints of its axis; the Binet formula
turns the eigenvalue into the exact growth constant, with $c_{n}$ the nearest integer to
$\alpha\lambda^{n}$; and in the spin representation the fundamental unit itself is the eigenvalue.

\subsection{What is false, and how sharply} The monoid is not conjugate into a Hilbert modular
group (integral traces); the boundary Hecke spectrum is exactly $\{0,3\}$, excluding the units; the
$\Q(\sqrt2)$-locus is a single boundary point; and even granting the eigenvalues, both the Ramanujan
bound $2\sqrt2$ and the Satake product condition $\alpha\beta=q=2$ fail. The correct slogan: the
Berggren tree is a $\Q$-arithmetic object whose hyperbolic elements have real quadratic multipliers;
$\Q(\sqrt2)$ is an eigenvalue field, not a field of definition.

\subsection{Applications} Theorem \ref{thm:unitlocus} is an address-level classification of the
almost-isoceles Pythagorean triples: they are exactly the $B$-words, and Theorem \ref{thm:binet}
gives their closed form. The relation $TU=3\,\mathrm{id}$ is the exact $3$-regularity of the tree
and, with the growth signatures of Section \ref{sec:trichotomy}, yields exact counts of nodes below
a hypotenuse bound. Methodologically, the refutation is a case study in distinguishing the
\emph{shape} of a local $L$-factor from its \emph{kind}: the invariant trace field and the Satake
normalization are cheap to compute and decisive.

\subsection{Future directions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Correct automorphic comparison.} Compare the tree with the automorphic theory of
$\mathrm{O}(2,1;\Z)\sim\mathrm{GL}(2,\Z)$ over $\Q$ --- classical modular and Maass forms --- and
ask which classical spectral data are visible in the Bernoulli measure on the boundary.
\item \emph{Other hyperbolic words.} Every word containing a $B$ and another letter has its own
trace $t$ and multiplier field $\Q(\sqrt{t^{2}-4})$. Classify which real quadratic fields arise, and
with what density: a Berggren analogue of trace-field statistics for $\mathrm{SL}(2,\Z)$.
\item \emph{Equidistribution.} Study the distribution of $|a-b|/c$ under the Bernoulli measure; the
unit locus is its extreme point and the full law should be a self-similar measure computable from
the three-letter transfer operator.
\item \emph{Weighted transfer operators.} Deform to
$T_{s}f(w)=\sum_{x}\|x\frown w\|^{-s}f(x\frown w)$ using hypotenuse growth as a weight; the
resulting Ruelle operator has a non-trivial spectrum and defines a dynamical zeta function --- the
correct $L$-function of the object, in contrast to the mirage factor $1-6x+x^{2}$.
\item \emph{Higher Pell families.} Repeat the analysis for Barning-type trees attached to
$x^{2}+y^{2}=2z^{2}$ or to Heronian triangles, where the analogous coordinate lands in
$\Z[\sqrt3]$ or $\Z[\sqrt5]$, and determine whether any such tree has an irrational trace field.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

The Berggren tree contains a genuine real quadratic thread: the silver coordinate, the unit orbit
along the spine, the negative Pell equation, the eigenvalue $3+2\sqrt2=(1+\sqrt2)^{2}$, and an
Euler-factor-shaped polynomial $1-6x+x^{2}$. It does not contain a Hilbert modular structure. Its
trace field is $\Q$; its boundary Hecke algebra has the two-point spectrum $\{0,3\}$; and its
$\Q(\sqrt2)$-locus is a single geodesic axis whose boundary trace is one point. The quadratic field
is the multiplier field of one hyperbolic letter in a three-letter alphabet whose other two letters
are parabolics fixing rational cusps.

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import isqrt, sqrt
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]
Quad = Tuple[int, int]  # x + y*sqrt(2)  <->  (x, y)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The three Berggren generators (integral isometries of a^2 + b^2 - c^2)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

MAT_A: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
MAT_B: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
MAT_C: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))

GENERATORS: Dict[str, Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...]] = {"A": MAT_A, "B": MAT_B, "C": MAT_C}
ROOT: Triple = (3, 4, 5)


def apply_matrix(m: Sequence[Sequence[int]], v: Triple) -> Triple:
    """Apply a 3x3 integer matrix to a triple."""
    return (
        m[0][0] * v[0] + m[0][1] * v[1] + m[0][2] * v[2],
        m[1][0] * v[0] + m[1][1] * v[1] + m[1][2] * v[2],
        m[2][0] * v[0] + m[2][1] * v[1] + m[2][2] * v[2],
    )


def apply_word(word: str, v: Triple = ROOT) -> Triple:
    """Apply the letters of `word` (left-to-right, outermost first) to `v`."""
    out = v
    for letter in reversed(word):
        out = apply_matrix(GENERATORS[letter], out)
    return out


def is_pythagorean(v: Triple) -> bool:
    a, b, c = v
    return a * a + b * b == c * c


def preserves_lorentz(m: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> bool:
    """Check M^T diag(1,1,-1) M = diag(1,1,-1)."""
    q = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, -1]]
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            s = sum(m[k][i] * q[k][k] * m[k][j] for k in range(3))
            if s != q[i][j]:
                return False
    return True


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact arithmetic in Z[sqrt 2]
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def z2_mul(u: Quad, v: Quad) -> Quad:
    """(x1 + y1 r2)(x2 + y2 r2) = (x1x2 + 2 y1y2) + (x1y2 + x2y1) r2."""
    return (u[0] * v[0] + 2 * u[1] * v[1], u[0] * v[1] + u[1] * v[0])


def z2_pow(u: Quad, n: int) -> Quad:
    out: Quad = (1, 0)
    base = u
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:
            out = z2_mul(out, base)
        base = z2_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return out


def z2_norm(u: Quad) -> int:
    """N(x + y sqrt2) = x^2 - 2 y^2."""
    return u[0] * u[0] - 2 * u[1] * u[1]


def z2_is_unit(u: Quad) -> bool:
    return z2_norm(u) in (1, -1)


def z2_float(u: Quad) -> float:
    return u[0] + u[1] * sqrt(2.0)


def silver_coordinate(v: Triple) -> Quad:
    """zeta(a,b,c) = (a+b) + c sqrt2."""
    a, b, c = v
    return (a + b, c)


SILVER: Quad = (1, 1)        # 1 + sqrt2, the fundamental unit
LAMBDA: Quad = (3, 2)        # 3 + 2 sqrt2 = (1 + sqrt2)^2
LAMBDA_BAR: Quad = (3, -2)   # 3 - 2 sqrt2


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The tree, its spine, and the unit locus
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def words(depth: int) -> Iterator[str]:
    """All addresses of length exactly `depth` (empty word for depth 0)."""
    if depth == 0:
        yield ""
        return
    for tup in product("ABC", repeat=depth):
        yield "".join(tup)


def spine(n: int) -> Triple:
    """n-th node of the all-B branch."""
    return apply_word("B" * n)


def leg_difference(v: Triple) -> int:
    return v[0] - v[1]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The boundary Hecke algebra at finite depth
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def hecke_matrix_depth(k: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """
    Matrix of H = U T restricted to observables depending only on the first k letters
    of a boundary address, in the basis of depth-k cylinder indicators.

    On the boundary, (T f)(w) = sum_x f(x w) and (U f)(w) = f(sigma w), so
      (H f)(w) = (U T f)(w) = sum_x f(x . sigma w) = sum_x f(x w1 w2 ... ),
    which only ever reads the first k letters of w if f does.  Hence H preserves the
    depth-k subspace and acts there by the displayed matrix.
    """
    idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(words(k))}
    n = len(idx)
    mat = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for w, i in idx.items():
        tail = w[1:]                      # drop first letter: sigma w
        for x in "ABC":
            j = idx[x + tail]             # prepend x
            mat[i][j] += 1
    return mat


def matrix_eigenvalues_integer(mat: List[List[int]]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """
    Exact spectrum for the specific structure at hand: H satisfies H^2 = 3H, so its
    eigenvalues are 0 and 3.  We verify H^2 = 3H exactly and compute multiplicities
    as rank(H) (eigenvalue 3) and n - rank(H) (eigenvalue 0).
    """
    n = len(mat)
    sq = [[sum(mat[i][t] * mat[t][j] for t in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    assert all(sq[i][j] == 3 * mat[i][j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n)), "H^2 = 3H failed"
    r = rank_fraction([[Fraction(x) for x in row] for row in mat])
    return {3: r, 0: n - r}


def rank_fraction(mat: List[List[Fraction]]) -> int:
    """Exact rank by Gaussian elimination over the rationals."""
    m = [row[:] for row in mat]
    rows, cols = len(m), len(m[0])
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = None
        for i in range(r, rows):
            if m[i][c] != 0:
                piv = i
                break
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        inv = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / inv for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [a - f * b for a, b in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return r

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import isqrt, sqrt
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]
Quad = Tuple[int, int]  # x + y*sqrt(2)  <->  (x, y)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The three Berggren generators (integral isometries of a^2 + b^2 - c^2)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

MAT_A: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
MAT_B: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
MAT_C: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))

GENERATORS: Dict[str, Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...]] = {"A": MAT_A, "B": MAT_B, "C": MAT_C}
ROOT: Triple = (3, 4, 5)


def apply_matrix(m: Sequence[Sequence[int]], v: Triple) -> Triple:
    """Apply a 3x3 integer matrix to a triple."""
    return (
        m[0][0] * v[0] + m[0][1] * v[1] + m[0][2] * v[2],
        m[1][0] * v[0] + m[1][1] * v[1] + m[1][2] * v[2],
        m[2][0] * v[0] + m[2][1] * v[1] + m[2][2] * v[2],
    )


def apply_word(word: str, v: Triple = ROOT) -> Triple:
    """Apply the letters of `word` (left-to-right, outermost first) to `v`."""
    out = v
    for letter in reversed(word):
        out = apply_matrix(GENERATORS[letter], out)
    return out


def is_pythagorean(v: Triple) -> bool:
    a, b, c = v
    return a * a + b * b == c * c


def preserves_lorentz(m: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> bool:
    """Check M^T diag(1,1,-1) M = diag(1,1,-1)."""
    q = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, -1]]
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            s = sum(m[k][i] * q[k][k] * m[k][j] for k in range(3))
            if s != q[i][j]:
                return False
    return True


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact arithmetic in Z[sqrt 2]
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def z2_mul(u: Quad, v: Quad) -> Quad:
    """(x1 + y1 r2)(x2 + y2 r2) = (x1x2 + 2 y1y2) + (x1y2 + x2y1) r2."""
    return (u[0] * v[0] + 2 * u[1] * v[1], u[0] * v[1] + u[1] * v[0])


def z2_pow(u: Quad, n: int) -> Quad:
    out: Quad = (1, 0)
    base = u
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:
            out = z2_mul(out, base)
        base = z2_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return out


def z2_norm(u: Quad) -> int:
    """N(x + y sqrt2) = x^2 - 2 y^2."""
    return u[0] * u[0] - 2 * u[1] * u[1]


def z2_is_unit(u: Quad) -> bool:
    return z2_norm(u) in (1, -1)


def z2_float(u: Quad) -> float:
    return u[0] + u[1] * sqrt(2.0)


def silver_coordinate(v: Triple) -> Quad:
    """zeta(a,b,c) = (a+b) + c sqrt2."""
    a, b, c = v
    return (a + b, c)


SILVER: Quad = (1, 1)        # 1 + sqrt2, the fundamental unit
LAMBDA: Quad = (3, 2)        # 3 + 2 sqrt2 = (1 + sqrt2)^2
LAMBDA_BAR: Quad = (3, -2)   # 3 - 2 sqrt2


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The tree, its spine, and the unit locus
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def words(depth: int) -> Iterator[str]:
    """All addresses of length exactly `depth` (empty word for depth 0)."""
    if depth == 0:
        yield ""
        return
    for tup in product("ABC", repeat=depth):
        yield "".join(tup)


def spine(n: int) -> Triple:
    """n-th node of the all-B branch."""
    return apply_word("B" * n)


def leg_difference(v: Triple) -> int:
    return v[0] - v[1]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The boundary Hecke algebra at finite depth
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def hecke_matrix_depth(k: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """
    Matrix of H = U T restricted to observables depending only on the first k letters
    of a boundary address, in the basis of depth-k cylinder indicators.

    On the boundary, (T f)(w) = sum_x f(x w) and (U f)(w) = f(sigma w), so
      (H f)(w) = (U T f)(w) = sum_x f(x . sigma w) = sum_x f(x w1 w2 ... ),
    which only ever reads the first k letters of w if f does.  Hence H preserves the
    depth-k subspace and acts there by the displayed matrix.
    """
    idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(words(k))}
    n = len(idx)
    mat = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for w, i in idx.items():
        tail = w[1:]                      # drop first letter: sigma w
        for x in "ABC":
            j = idx[x + tail]             # prepend x
            mat[i][j] += 1
    return mat


def matrix_eigenvalues_integer(mat: List[List[int]]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """
    Exact spectrum for the specific structure at hand: H satisfies H^2 = 3H, so its
    eigenvalues are 0 and 3.  We verify H^2 = 3H exactly and compute multiplicities
    as rank(H) (eigenvalue 3) and n - rank(H) (eigenvalue 0).
    """
    n = len(mat)
    sq = [[sum(mat[i][t] * mat[t][j] for t in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    assert all(sq[i][j] == 3 * mat[i][j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n)), "H^2 = 3H failed"
    r = rank_fraction([[Fraction(x) for x in row] for row in mat])
    return {3: r, 0: n - r}


def rank_fraction(mat: List[List[Fraction]]) -> int:
    """Exact rank by Gaussian elimination over the rationals."""
    m = [row[:] for row in mat]
    rows, cols = len(m), len(m[0])
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = None
        for i in range(r, rows):
            if m[i][c] != 0:
                piv = i
                break
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        inv = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / inv for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [a - f * b for a, b in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return r

from itertools import product

Mat2 = Tuple[int, int, int, int]  # (m00, m01, m10, m11)

SPIN: Dict[str, Mat2] = {
    "A": (2, -1, 1, 0),
    "B": (2, 1, 1, 0),
    "C": (1, 2, 0, 1),
}


def mat_mul(x: Mat2, y: Mat2) -> Mat2:
    return (
        x[0] * y[0] + x[1] * y[2], x[0] * y[1] + x[1] * y[3],
        x[2] * y[0] + x[3] * y[2], x[2] * y[1] + x[3] * y[3],
    )


def word_matrix(word: str) -> Mat2:
    out: Mat2 = (1, 0, 0, 1)
    for letter in word:
        out = mat_mul(out, SPIN[letter])
    return out


def squarefree_part(n: int) -> int:
    """Largest squarefree divisor d with n = d * square (n > 0)."""
    d = 1
    m = n
    p = 2
    while p * p <= m:
        e = 0
        while m % p == 0:
            m //= p
            e += 1
        if e % 2 == 1:
            d *= p
        p += 1
    return d * m


def multiplier_field(word: str) -> Tuple[int, int, str]:
    """Return (trace, determinant, name of the multiplier field)."""
    m = word_matrix(word)
    t = m[0] + m[3]
    det = m[0] * m[3] - m[1] * m[2]
    disc = t * t - 4 * det
    if disc < 0:
        return t, det, "elliptic (complex multiplier)"
    if disc == 0:
        return t, det, "parabolic (multiplier 1)"
    d = squarefree_part(disc)
    if d == 1:
        return t, det, "split over Q (rational multiplier)"
    return t, det, f"Q(sqrt {d})"

            _, _, field = multiplier_field(w)
            counts[field] += 1
            examples.setdefault(field, w)
    print(f"Words of length 1..{max_len}: {sum(counts.values())}")
    print(f"{'multiplier field':>34} {'count':>7} {'example word':>14}")
    for field, c in counts.most_common():
        print(f"{field:>34} {c:>7} {examples[field]:>14}")

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import deque
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, NamedTuple, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]
Quad = Tuple[int, int]  # x + y*sqrt(2)

MAT: Dict[str, Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...]] = {
    "A": ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3)),
    "B": ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3)),
    "C": ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3)),
}
ROOT: Triple = (3, 4, 5)


class Node(NamedTuple):
    address: str
    triple: Triple
    zeta: Quad
    norm: int
    is_unit: bool


def _apply(letter: str, v: Triple) -> Triple:
    m = MAT[letter]
    return (
        m[0][0] * v[0] + m[0][1] * v[1] + m[0][2] * v[2],
        m[1][0] * v[0] + m[1][1] * v[1] + m[1][2] * v[2],
        m[2][0] * v[0] + m[2][1] * v[1] + m[2][2] * v[2],
    )


def _silver(v: Triple) -> Quad:
    return (v[0] + v[1], v[2])


def _norm(z: Quad) -> int:
    return z[0] * z[0] - 2 * z[1] * z[1]


def traverse(max_depth: int) -> Iterator[Node]:
    """Breadth-first traversal to `max_depth`; yields (3^(d+1)-1)/2 nodes."""
    queue: deque = deque([("", ROOT)])
    while queue:
        address, v = queue.popleft()
        z = _silver(v)
        n = _norm(z)
        yield Node(address, v, z, n, abs(n) == 1)
        if len(address) < max_depth:
            for letter in "ABC":
                queue.append((letter + address, _apply(letter, v)))


def unit_nodes(max_depth: int) -> List[str]:
    """Addresses whose silver coordinate is a unit of Z[sqrt 2]."""
    return [node.address for node in traverse(max_depth) if node.is_unit]

elimination.  Cost: O(9^k) integer operations for the square, O(27^k) worst case for
the elimination, which is fine for k <= 6.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[int]]


def cylinder_words(k: int) -> List[str]:
    """All addresses of length k, i.e. the depth-k cylinders."""
    return ["".join(t) for t in product("ABC", repeat=k)]


def hecke_matrix(k: int) -> Matrix:
    """Matrix of H = U T on depth-k cylinder observables: (Hf)(w) = sum_x f(x sigma w)."""
    idx: Dict[str, int] = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(cylinder_words(k))}
    n = len(idx)
    mat: Matrix = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for w, i in idx.items():
        tail = w[1:]
        for x in "ABC":
            mat[i][idx[x + tail]] += 1
    return mat


def matrix_square(mat: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    n = len(mat)
    return [[sum(mat[i][t] * mat[t][j] for t in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def exact_rank(mat: Matrix) -> int:
    """Rank over Q by fraction-free-free Gaussian elimination with Fraction pivots."""
    m: List[List[Fraction]] = [[Fraction(x) for x in row] for row in mat]
    rows, cols = len(m), len(m[0])
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = next((i for i in range(r, rows) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        inv = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / inv for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [a - f * b for a, b in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return r


def certify_spectrum(k: int) -> Tuple[bool, int, int]:
    """Return (H^2 == 3H, multiplicity of eigenvalue 3, multiplicity of eigenvalue 0)."""
    mat = hecke_matrix(k)
    n = len(mat)
    sq = matrix_square(mat)
    idempotent = all(sq[i][j] == 3 * mat[i][j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n))
    r = exact_rank(mat)
    return idempotent, r, n - r


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"{'k':>3} {'dim':>6} {'H^2 = 3H':>10} {'mult(3)':>9} {'mult(0)':>9} {'other':>7}")

ROOT: Triple = (3, 4, 5)
DEPTH = 7


def apply_letter(letter: str, v: Triple) -> Triple:
    m = MAT[letter]
    return (
        m[0][0] * v[0] + m[0][1] * v[1] + m[0][2] * v[2],
        m[1][0] * v[0] + m[1][1] * v[1] + m[1][2] * v[2],
        m[2][0] * v[0] + m[2][1] * v[1] + m[2][2] * v[2],
    )


def build() -> List[Tuple[str, Triple, float, float]]:
    """Return (address, triple, x, y) for every node up to DEPTH, radial layout."""
    nodes: List[Tuple[str, Triple, float, float]] = [("", ROOT, 0.0, 0.0)]
    frontier: List[Tuple[str, Triple, float, float]] = [("", ROOT, 0.0, 2.0 * math.pi)]
    depth = 0
    while depth < DEPTH:
        new_frontier = []
        for address, v, lo, hi in frontier:
            width = (hi - lo) / 3.0
            for i, letter in enumerate("ABC"):
                child_lo = lo + i * width
                child_hi = child_lo + width
                child = apply_letter(letter, v)
                theta = 0.5 * (child_lo + child_hi)
                r = depth + 1
                nodes.append((letter + address, child, r * math.cos(theta), r * math.sin(theta)))

    print("wrote berggren_tree_unit_locus.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

def step_B(v: Triple) -> Triple:
    a, b, c = v
    return (a + 2 * b + 2 * c, 2 * a + b + 2 * c, 2 * a + 2 * b + 3 * c)


def step_C(v: Triple) -> Triple:
    a, b, c = v
    return (-a + 2 * b + 2 * c, -2 * a + b + 2 * c, -2 * a + 2 * b + 3 * c)


def branch(step, n_max: int) -> List[Triple]:
    v: Triple = (3, 4, 5)
    out = [v]
    for _ in range(n_max):

        out.append(v)
    return out

*A guided tour: from the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle to Hecke operators on a Cantor set — and to a
precise account of why one very beautiful conjecture is false.*

---

## 0 · The one picture to keep in mind

Take the triangle $(3,4,5)$. Apply three fixed integer matrices to it. Each output is again a
right triangle with whole-number sides. Repeat forever, and you get a tree in which **every**
primitive Pythagorean triple appears exactly once, with a unique address like $BBAC$ in the
alphabet $\{A, B, C\}$.

$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}, \qquad
C = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$$

All three preserve $a^2 + b^2 - c^2$, so they are integral symmetries of the light cone of
$2{+}1$-dimensional spacetime. This tree is classical — it goes back to work of
[Berggren, Barning and Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_of_primitive_Pythagorean_triples)
— but the question we ask about it is not.

<details>
<summary><b>Why is the tree free, and what does that give us?</b></summary>

Freeness means the map (word) $\mapsto$ (triple) is a bijection: distinct addresses give distinct
triples, and every primitive triple with even second leg is hit. Consequently the tree has a
well-defined **boundary at infinity**: the set $\{A,B,C\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ of infinite addresses.
With the product topology this is a Cantor set — a "$3$-adic" Cantor set — carrying the natural
Bernoulli measure giving each length-$n$ cylinder mass $3^{-n}$. Boundaries of regular trees are
where local Hecke theory lives, which is exactly why the question below is tempting.
</details>

---

## 1 · Walk the tree yourself

Before any theory, get your hands on the object. Press $B$ repeatedly, and watch the two legs stay
one apart: $(3,4,5)$, $(21,20,29)$, $(119,120,169)$, $(697,696,985)$. Then insert a single $A$ and
watch that near-isoceles property vanish and never come back.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

The quantity being tracked is the **silver coordinate**

$$\zeta(a,b,c) = (a+b) + c\sqrt{2} \in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{2}],$$

an element of the ring of integers of the real quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$. Its norm is
$N(x + y\sqrt2) = x^2 - 2y^2$, and on the light cone something lovely happens:

$$N(\zeta(a,b,c)) = (a+b)^2 - 2c^2 = -(a-b)^2 .$$

So $\zeta$ is a **unit** of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ precisely when $|a-b| = 1$.

---

## 2 · Why the middle letter is special

Compute what the generators do to $\zeta$. The answer is the heart of the whole story:

$$\zeta(Bv) = (3 + 2\sqrt2)\,\zeta(v), \qquad
\zeta(Av) = (3+2\sqrt2)\bigl((a-b) + c\sqrt2\bigr), \qquad
\zeta(Cv) = (3+2\sqrt2)\bigl((b-a) + c\sqrt2\bigr).$$

Only $B$ acts by pure multiplication on its own coordinate — and the multiplier is
$3 + 2\sqrt2 = (1+\sqrt2)^2$, the **square of the fundamental unit** of $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$.
Since $\zeta(3,4,5) = 7 + 5\sqrt2 = (1+\sqrt2)^3$, the $n$-th node of the all-$B$ spine has

$$\zeta = (1+\sqrt2)^{2n+3},$$

so the spine *is* the odd part of the unit group, and $N(\zeta) = -1$ says the spine solves the
**negative Pell equation** $(a+b)^2 - 2c^2 = -1$.

<details>
<summary><b>The proof, in three lines</b></summary>

The first two coordinates of $Bv$ sum to $3(a+b) + 4c$, and the third is $2(a+b) + 3c$. Hence
$$\zeta(Bv) = \bigl(3(a+b)+4c\bigr) + \bigl(2(a+b)+3c\bigr)\sqrt2
= (3+2\sqrt2)\bigl((a+b) + c\sqrt2\bigr),$$
where the last equality is the multiplication rule $(x + y\sqrt2)(3+2\sqrt2) = (3x+4y) + (2x+3y)\sqrt2$.
For $A$ and $C$ the same computation applies with $a-b$ or $b-a$ in place of $a+b$: the leg sum and
leg difference get swapped, which is exactly why those letters leave the unit locus.
</details>

## 3 · Where the field lives: one geodesic, not a boundary

The dynamics of the leg difference $d = a - b$ is brutally simple:

$$A: d \mapsto -(a+b), \qquad B: d \mapsto -d, \qquad C: d \mapsto a+b .$$

Since every node of the tree has $a + b \ge 7$, the letters $A$ and $C$ throw $|d|$ up to at least
$7$, and it can only grow after that. So:

> **Unit Locus Theorem.** A node has unit silver coordinate — equivalently is almost-isoceles,
> equivalently solves the negative Pell equation — **if and only if its address is a word in the
> single letter $B$**. In the boundary Cantor set, the unit locus is the single point $BBB\cdots$.

One point of Hausdorff dimension $0$ inside a Cantor set of full dimension. The picture below
makes this visible: the red ray is the entire $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$-locus of the tree.

| tree regularity | $q + 1 = 3$, so $q = 2$ |

And the hypotenuses of the spine satisfy $c_{n+2} = 6c_{n+1} - c_n$, whose reciprocal polynomial is

$$1 - 6x + x^2 = \bigl(1 - (3+2\sqrt2)x\bigr)\bigl(1 - (3-2\sqrt2)x\bigr)$$

— exactly the shape of an unramified local Euler factor with Satake parameters $3 \pm 2\sqrt2$.

> **The conjecture.** The boundary of the Berggren tree carries automorphic forms for a
> [Hilbert modular group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_modular_form) over
> $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, with a Hecke eigenbasis whose eigenvalues are the silver units — placing

> [Langlands program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_program).

It is false. What follows is the pleasure of finding out exactly how.

## 5 · Obstruction I — the tree is rational

Arithmetic groups carry an invariant no change of coordinates can hide: the field generated by
traces. The Berggren generators are integer matrices, with $\operatorname{tr} A = \operatorname{tr} C = 3$
and $\operatorname{tr} B = 5$. Products of integer matrices are integer matrices, so **every**
element of the monoid has an integer trace. But the Hilbert modular group
$\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2])$ contains $\begin{pmatrix}1+\sqrt2 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$
of trace $1+\sqrt2$, whose three-dimensional adjoint has trace $2 + 2\sqrt2$ — irrational. Trace
is conjugation invariant, so that element is not conjugate into the Berggren monoid, in any
coordinates at all.

The invariant trace field is $\mathbb{Q}$. To see that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ is nevertheless a
perfectly real *eigenvalue* field — one of many — run the survey below, which computes the
multiplier field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{t^2 - 4\det})$ of every word up to a given length:

$\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ here.

---

## 6 · Obstruction II — the boundary's Hecke algebra is degenerate

Forget groups; build the Hecke theory directly on the boundary. Let observables be real functions
on $\{A,B,C\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and define

$$(Tf)(w) = \sum_{x \in \{A,B,C\}} f(x \frown w) \quad \text{(transfer / Hecke)},
\qquad (Uf)(w) = f(\sigma w) \quad \text{(shift)},$$

where $x \frown w$ prepends a letter and $\sigma$ deletes the first one. Deleting the letter you
just prepended returns you where you started, so

$$TU = 3\,\mathrm{id}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad H := UT \ \text{satisfies}\ H^2 = 3H .$$

That single quadratic relation decides everything: $E = \tfrac13 H$ is idempotent, observables
split canonically as $\operatorname{im}U \oplus \ker T$, and:

> **Spectral Dichotomy.** If $f \neq 0$ and $Hf = \mu f$ then $\mu = 0$ or $\mu = 3$. The spectrum
> of the boundary Hecke operator is exactly $\{0,3\}$. In particular the silver units
> $3 \pm 2\sqrt2 \approx 5.828,\ 0.172$ are **not** Hecke eigenvalues.

Do not take my word for it — certify it at any depth:

<details>
<summary><b>The one-line proof, and why both eigenvalues really occur</b></summary>

Apply $H$ to $Hf = \mu f$: on one hand $H^2f = \mu^2 f$, on the other $H^2 f = 3Hf = 3\mu f$.
Since $f \neq 0$, $\mu(\mu - 3) = 0$.

Both values occur. The constant observable $\mathbf1$ has $H\mathbf1 = 3\mathbf1$: this is the
trivial, or *Eisenstein*, eigenform of a $(q+1)$-regular tree, with the degree eigenvalue
$q + 1 = 3$. And the "first letter" observable with values $+1$ on $A$, $-1$ on $B$, $0$ on $C$ is
killed by $T$, hence by $H$. So the boundary carries a genuine Hecke algebra — a rank-one Hecke
pair — but a degenerate one: the only nonzero eigenvalue is the trivial one, and there is no
family of eigenforms to be an automorphic spectrum.
</details>

## 7 · Obstruction III — even hypothetically, the numbers are wrong

Suppose the units *were* eigenvalues. Two normalization invariants still fail.

**Temperedness.** The [Ramanujan–Petersson bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%E2%80%93Petersson_conjecture)
for a tempered local Hecke eigenvalue at a prime with residue field of size $q$ is
$|\mu| \le 2\sqrt q$. Here $q = 2$, so the window is $[-2\sqrt2, 2\sqrt2] \approx [-2.83, 2.83]$ —
and both $3$ and $3 + 2\sqrt2$ lie outside it.

**Satake product.** An unramified representation of $\mathrm{GL}(2)$ with trivial central character
has Satake parameters multiplying to $q$. But

$$(3+2\sqrt2)(3-2\sqrt2) = 9 - 8 = 1 \neq 2 .$$

The product is $1$ precisely because $3 \pm 2\sqrt2$ are conjugate **units of norm one**. Beautiful
arithmetic; wrong normalization. The polynomial $1 - 6x + x^2$ is the Euler factor of a real
quadratic unit, not of a Hilbert modular form.

---

## 8 · So what *is* the tree?

The answer comes from a spectral trichotomy of the three-letter alphabet.

- $A$ and $C$ have characteristic polynomial $(X-1)^3$ with $(A-I)^3 = 0 \neq (A-I)^2$: they are
  **parabolic**, and each fixes a *rational* point of the light cone, $(0,1,1)$ and $(1,0,1)$.
  Their branches grow only quadratically:
  $A^n(3,4,5) = (2n+3,\,2n^2+6n+4,\,2n^2+6n+5)$ and $C^n(3,4,5) = (4n^2+8n+3,\,4n+4,\,4n^2+8n+5)$.
- $B$ is **hyperbolic**, with eigenvalues $-1, 3\pm2\sqrt2$ and light-like eigenvectors
  $(1,1,\pm\sqrt2)$ — quadratic irrational, with no rational light-like eigendirection at all. Its
  branch grows exponentially, and the hypotenuse is the *nearest integer* to
  $\frac{7+5\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}(3+2\sqrt2)^n$, while the direction $(a+b)/c$ approaches $\sqrt2$ with
  the exact error law $\bigl((a+b)/c\bigr)^2 = 2 - 1/c^2$.

That is a better outcome than a vague positive result would have been. Five suggestive

the two invariants that actually decide such questions: the **trace field** of the group and the

the right *kind*.

/-! ### The fundamental unit of `ℤ[√2]` -/

/-- The fundamental unit `1 + √2` of `ℤ[√2]` (the *silver ratio*). -/
def silver : ℤ√2 := ⟨1, 1⟩

/-- The square `3 + 2√2` of the fundamental unit: the hyperbolic eigenvalue of the
Berggren generator `mB`. -/
def lam : ℤ√2 := ⟨3, 2⟩

/-- `√2` itself, as an element of `ℤ[√2]`. -/
def rt2 : ℤ√2 := ⟨0, 1⟩

theorem rt2_sq : rt2 * rt2 = 2 := by decide

theorem lam_eq_silver_sq : lam = silver ^ 2 := by decide

theorem silver_norm : silver.norm = -1 := by decide

theorem lam_norm : lam.norm = 1 := by decide

theorem lam_isUnit : IsUnit lam := IsUnit.of_mul_eq_one (⟨3, -2⟩ : ℤ√2) (by decide)

theorem silver_isUnit : IsUnit silver := IsUnit.of_mul_eq_one (⟨-1, 1⟩ : ℤ√2) (by decide)

/-- Norms are multiplicative on powers. -/
theorem norm_pow (x : ℤ√2) : ∀ n : ℕ, (x ^ n).norm = x.norm ^ n := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih => rw [pow_succ, pow_succ, Zsqrtd.norm_mul, ih]

/-- Odd powers of the fundamental unit have norm `−1`: they are the solutions of the
negative Pell equation `x² − 2y² = −1`. -/
theorem norm_silver_odd (n : ℕ) : (silver ^ (2 * n + 3)).norm = -1 := by
  rw [norm_pow, silver_norm]
  rw [show 2 * n + 3 = 2 * (n + 1) + 1 by ring, pow_succ, pow_mul]
  norm_num

/-! ### The silver coordinate of a Lorentz vector -/

/-- The **silver coordinate** `ζ(a, b, c) = (a + b) + c√2 ∈ ℤ[√2]`. -/
def zeta (v : Vec) : ℤ√2 := ⟨v.1 + v.2.1, v.2.2⟩

/-- The twisted silver coordinate `ζ⁻(a, b, c) = (a − b) + c√2`. -/
def zetaMinus (v : Vec) : ℤ√2 := ⟨v.1 - v.2.1, v.2.2⟩

/-- **The hyperbolic generator is multiplication by the square of the fundamental unit.**
This is the key intertwining relation of the whole file; note that it holds for *every*
integer vector, not just for Pythagorean triples. -/
theorem zeta_mB (v : Vec) : zeta (mB v) = lam * zeta v := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, c⟩ := v
  ext <;> simp [zeta, mB, lam, Zsqrtd.re_mul, Zsqrtd.im_mul] <;> ring

/-- `mA` multiplies by the same unit but *reads the twisted coordinate*: the `ℤ[√2]`-scalar
structure is not preserved by this generator. -/
theorem zeta_mA (v : Vec) : zeta (mA v) = lam * zetaMinus v := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, c⟩ := v
  ext <;> simp [zeta, zetaMinus, mA, lam, Zsqrtd.re_mul, Zsqrtd.im_mul] <;> ring

/-- `mC` multiplies by the same unit after the *opposite* twist. -/
theorem zeta_mC (v : Vec) : zeta (mC v) = lam * ⟨v.2.1 - v.1, v.2.2⟩ := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, c⟩ := v
  ext <;> simp [zeta, mC, lam, Zsqrtd.re_mul, Zsqrtd.im_mul] <;> ring

/-! ### Admissible nodes -/

/-- The geometric invariant satisfied by every node of the Berggren tree: a genuine
right triangle with positive legs shorter than the hypotenuse. -/
def Adm (v : Vec) : Prop := 0 < v.1 ∧ 0 < v.2.1 ∧ v.1 < v.2.2 ∧ v.2.1 < v.2.2

theorem adm_root : Adm root := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> simp [root]

theorem adm_mA {v : Vec} (h : Adm v) : Adm (mA v) := by
  obtain ⟨h1, h2, h3, h4⟩ := h
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> simp only [mA] <;> linarith

theorem adm_mB {v : Vec} (h : Adm v) : Adm (mB v) := by
  obtain ⟨h1, h2, h3, h4⟩ := h
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> simp only [mB] <;> linarith

theorem adm_mC {v : Vec} (h : Adm v) : Adm (mC v) := by
  obtain ⟨h1, h2, h3, h4⟩ := h
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> simp only [mC] <;> linarith

  cases x
  · exact adm_mA h
  · exact adm_mB h
  · exact adm_mC h

/-- On the light cone the `ℤ[√2]`-norm of the silver coordinate is minus the square of the
leg difference. -/
theorem zeta_norm_eq_neg_sq {v : Vec} (h : OnCone v) :

  obtain ⟨a, b, c⟩ := v
  rw [onCone_iff] at h
  simp only [zeta, Zsqrtd.norm_def]
  nlinarith [h]

theorem diff_mB (v : Vec) : (mB v).1 - (mB v).2.1 = -(v.1 - v.2.1) := by

/-- The one-sided shift: forget the first letter of an address. -/
def shift (w : Bdry) : Bdry := fun n => w (n + 1)

/-- Prepend a letter to an address (descend one level in the tree). -/
def cons (x : Gen) (w : Bdry) : Bdry := fun n => Nat.casesOn n x w

@[simp] theorem cons_zero (x : Gen) (w : Bdry) : cons x w 0 = x := rfl

and the three obstructions to automorphy.

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import isqrt, sqrt
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

Triple = Tuple[int, int, int]
Quad = Tuple[int, int]  # x + y*sqrt(2)  <->  (x, y)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The three Berggren generators (integral isometries of a^2 + b^2 - c^2)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

MAT_A: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, -2, 2), (2, -1, 2), (2, -2, 3))
MAT_B: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((1, 2, 2), (2, 1, 2), (2, 2, 3))
MAT_C: Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...] = ((-1, 2, 2), (-2, 1, 2), (-2, 2, 3))

GENERATORS: Dict[str, Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], ...]] = {"A": MAT_A, "B": MAT_B, "C": MAT_C}
ROOT: Triple = (3, 4, 5)


def apply_matrix(m: Sequence[Sequence[int]], v: Triple) -> Triple:
    """Apply a 3x3 integer matrix to a triple."""
    return (
        m[0][0] * v[0] + m[0][1] * v[1] + m[0][2] * v[2],
        m[1][0] * v[0] + m[1][1] * v[1] + m[1][2] * v[2],
        m[2][0] * v[0] + m[2][1] * v[1] + m[2][2] * v[2],
    )


def apply_word(word: str, v: Triple = ROOT) -> Triple:
    """Apply the letters of `word` (left-to-right, outermost first) to `v`."""
    out = v
    for letter in reversed(word):
        out = apply_matrix(GENERATORS[letter], out)
    return out


def is_pythagorean(v: Triple) -> bool:
    a, b, c = v
    return a * a + b * b == c * c


def preserves_lorentz(m: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> bool:
    """Check M^T diag(1,1,-1) M = diag(1,1,-1)."""
    q = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, -1]]
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            s = sum(m[k][i] * q[k][k] * m[k][j] for k in range(3))
            if s != q[i][j]:
                return False
    return True


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact arithmetic in Z[sqrt 2]
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def z2_mul(u: Quad, v: Quad) -> Quad:
    """(x1 + y1 r2)(x2 + y2 r2) = (x1x2 + 2 y1y2) + (x1y2 + x2y1) r2."""
    return (u[0] * v[0] + 2 * u[1] * v[1], u[0] * v[1] + u[1] * v[0])


def z2_pow(u: Quad, n: int) -> Quad:
    out: Quad = (1, 0)
    base = u
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:
            out = z2_mul(out, base)
        base = z2_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return out


def z2_norm(u: Quad) -> int:
    """N(x + y sqrt2) = x^2 - 2 y^2."""
    return u[0] * u[0] - 2 * u[1] * u[1]


def z2_is_unit(u: Quad) -> bool:
    return z2_norm(u) in (1, -1)


def z2_float(u: Quad) -> float:
    return u[0] + u[1] * sqrt(2.0)


def silver_coordinate(v: Triple) -> Quad:
    """zeta(a,b,c) = (a+b) + c sqrt2."""
    a, b, c = v
    return (a + b, c)


SILVER: Quad = (1, 1)        # 1 + sqrt2, the fundamental unit
LAMBDA: Quad = (3, 2)        # 3 + 2 sqrt2 = (1 + sqrt2)^2
LAMBDA_BAR: Quad = (3, -2)   # 3 - 2 sqrt2


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The tree, its spine, and the unit locus
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def words(depth: int) -> Iterator[str]:
    """All addresses of length exactly `depth` (empty word for depth 0)."""
    if depth == 0:
        yield ""
        return
    for tup in product("ABC", repeat=depth):
        yield "".join(tup)


def spine(n: int) -> Triple:
    """n-th node of the all-B branch."""
    return apply_word("B" * n)


def leg_difference(v: Triple) -> int:
    return v[0] - v[1]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The boundary Hecke algebra at finite depth
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def hecke_matrix_depth(k: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """
    Matrix of H = U T restricted to observables depending only on the first k letters
    of a boundary address, in the basis of depth-k cylinder indicators.

    On the boundary, (T f)(w) = sum_x f(x w) and (U f)(w) = f(sigma w), so
      (H f)(w) = (U T f)(w) = sum_x f(x . sigma w) = sum_x f(x w1 w2 ... ),
    which only ever reads the first k letters of w if f does.  Hence H preserves the
    depth-k subspace and acts there by the displayed matrix.
    """
    idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(words(k))}
    n = len(idx)
    mat = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for w, i in idx.items():
        tail = w[1:]                      # drop first letter: sigma w
        for x in "ABC":
            j = idx[x + tail]             # prepend x
            mat[i][j] += 1
    return mat


def matrix_eigenvalues_integer(mat: List[List[int]]) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """
    Exact spectrum for the specific structure at hand: H satisfies H^2 = 3H, so its
    eigenvalues are 0 and 3.  We verify H^2 = 3H exactly and compute multiplicities
    as rank(H) (eigenvalue 3) and n - rank(H) (eigenvalue 0).
    """
    n = len(mat)
    sq = [[sum(mat[i][t] * mat[t][j] for t in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    assert all(sq[i][j] == 3 * mat[i][j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n)), "H^2 = 3H failed"
    r = rank_fraction([[Fraction(x) for x in row] for row in mat])
    return {3: r, 0: n - r}


def rank_fraction(mat: List[List[Fraction]]) -> int:
    """Exact rank by Gaussian elimination over the rationals."""
    m = [row[:] for row in mat]
    rows, cols = len(m), len(m[0])
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = None
        for i in range(r, rows):
            if m[i][c] != 0:
                piv = i
                break
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        inv = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / inv for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [a - f * b for a, b in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return r

```
/-
# The exchange metric on the chamber complex, its dual graph, and its f-vector

Cycle 2 of the single-voter exchange programme.  Building on
`Tropical/SocialChoice/{Chambers, ChamberComplex, SupportMatroid}.lean` and on
`Pythagorean/ExchangeLawSharp.lean`, we turn the exchange law into a *metric*
statement and read off the combinatorial invariants of the complex.

## The exchange metric

Fix a profile `x` sitting in the *open* chamber of the incumbent `i`, i.e.
`decisiveSet x = {i}`, and consider *downward* moves `y ≤ x` (a coalition of
voters lowers its scores; the others are untouched).  Call the set `D` of voters
that actually move the *exchange support* of the move.

* `decisiveSet_subset_of_le`: after a downward move, the decisive coalition is
  contained in `D ∪ decisiveSet x` — no voter outside the moving coalition can
  become decisive out of nowhere.
* `exchange_lower_bound`: to land in the cell labelled `T`, every voter of
  `T \ {i}` must move.
* `exchange_upper_bound`: and moving exactly the voters of `T \ {i}` suffices.
* `exchange_distance`: hence the **exchange distance from the chamber of `i` to
  the cell `T` is exactly `|T \ {i}|`** — an `IsLeast` statement, i.e. a sharp
  optimum, not just a pair of inequalities.
* `exchange_distance_eq_codim`: for a face `T` of the chamber of `i` this common
  value is `|T| - 1`, which by `SupportMatroid.finrank_cellDirection` is exactly
  the *codimension* of the cell.  Combinatorial distance = geometric
  codimension.

## The dual graph

* `exchangeGraph`, `exchangeGraph_eq_top`, `exchangeGraph_connected`,
  `exchangeGraph_isClique`: the graph on the support whose edges are the pairs
  of chambers separated by a wall is the *complete* graph; the complex is
  gallery-connected of diameter one.

## The f-vector and the Euler characteristic

* `card_labels_of_card`: the cells of codimension `d` are counted by
  `choose |S| (d+1)`.
* `card_cells`: the complex has exactly `2 ^ |S| - 1` cells.
* `euler_characteristic_eq_one`: the alternating sum of the f-vector is `1`:
  the chamber complex is Euler-contractible, as it must be, being a fan.

## Boundary

* `exchange_lower_bound_fails_for_raises`: an explicit two-voter example showing
  that the lower bound of the exchange metric really needs the moves to be
  downward — an upward move of the incumbent's own score changes the winner
  without touching the winner.
-/
import Mathlib
import Tropical.SocialChoice.SupportMatroid
import Pythagorean.ExchangeLawSharp

namespace PythagoreanExchangeGallery

open Finset TropicalChambers TropicalChamberComplex TropicalSupportMatroid
open PythagoreanExchangeLaw

variable {ι : Type*}

/-! ## Downward moves and the exchange metric -/

/-- **Locality of downward moves.**  If `y` is obtained from `x` by lowering the
scores of the voters in `D` only, then every voter decisive at `y` either moved
or was already decisive at `x`. -/
theorem decisiveSet_subset_of_le [DecidableEq ι] {S : Finset ι} (hS : S.Nonempty) (δ : ι → ℝ)
    {x y : ι → ℝ} {D : Finset ι} (hle : ∀ k, y k ≤ x k) (hoff : ∀ k ∉ D, y k = x k) :
    decisiveSet S hS δ y ⊆ D ∪ decisiveSet S hS δ x := by
  classical
  intro m hm
  by_cases hmD : m ∈ D
  · exact Finset.mem_union_left _ hmD
  refine Finset.mem_union_right _ ?_
  obtain ⟨hmS, hmval⟩ := mem_decisiveSet_iff.mp hm
  have hagg : tropAgg S hS δ y ≤ tropAgg S hS δ x := tropAgg_mono hS δ hle
  have hxm : y m = x m := hoff m hmD
  have hge : tropAgg S hS δ x ≤ x m + δ m := Finset.inf'_le (fun n => x n + δ n) hmS
  rw [hxm] at hmval
  exact mem_decisiveSet_iff.mpr ⟨hmS, le_antisymm (by linarith) hge⟩

/-- **Lower bound for the exchange metric.**  Starting from the open chamber of
`i`, any downward move landing in the cell labelled `T` must move every voter of
`T \ {i}`. -/
theorem exchange_lower_bound [DecidableEq ι] {S : Finset ι} (hS : S.Nonempty) (δ : ι → ℝ)
    {x y : ι → ℝ} {i : ι} {D T : Finset ι} (hxi : decisiveSet S hS δ x = {i})
    (hle : ∀ k, y k ≤ x k) (hoff : ∀ k ∉ D, y k = x k) (hy : decisiveSet S hS δ y = T) :
    T.erase i ⊆ D := by
  classical
  intro m hm
  obtain ⟨hmi, hmT⟩ := Finset.mem_erase.mp hm
  have := decisiveSet_subset_of_le hS δ (D := D) hle hoff (by rw [hy]; exact hmT)
  rcases Finset.mem_union.mp this with h | h
  · exact h
  · rw [hxi, Finset.mem_singleton] at h
    exact absurd h hmi

/-- **Upper bound for the exchange metric.**  Moving exactly the voters of
`T \ {i}` downwards suffices to reach the cell labelled `T`. -/
theorem exchange_upper_bound [DecidableEq ι] {S : Finset ι} (hS : S.Nonempty) (δ : ι → ℝ)
    {x : ι → ℝ} {i : ι} {T : Finset ι} (hxi : decisiveSet S hS δ x = {i})
    (hTS : T ⊆ S) (hT : T.Nonempty) :
    ∃ y : ι → ℝ, (∀ k, y k ≤ x k) ∧ (∀ k ∉ T.erase i, y k = x k) ∧
      decisiveSet S hS δ y = T := by
  classical
  have hi : i ∈ decisiveSet S hS δ x := by rw [hxi]; exact Finset.mem_singleton_self i
  have hx : x ∈ chamber S δ i := (mem_decisiveSet_iff_mem_chamber.mp hi).2
  by_cases hiT : i ∈ T
  · refine ⟨coalitionExchange δ x i (T.erase i) 0, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · intro k
      by_cases hk : k ∈ T.erase i
      · have hmono := coalitionExchange_monomial (δ := δ) (x := x) (i := i) (T := T.erase i)
          (ε := 0) hk
        have hchamber := hx k (hTS (Finset.mem_of_mem_erase hk))
        linarith
      · rw [coalitionExchange_eq_of_notMem hk]
    · intro k hk
      exact coalitionExchange_eq_of_notMem hk
    · rw [decisiveSet_coalitionExchange_wall hS δ (hTS hiT) hx
        ((Finset.erase_subset _ _).trans hTS), hxi]
      ext k
      simp only [Finset.mem_union, Finset.mem_erase, Finset.mem_singleton]
      constructor
      · rintro (⟨-, hk⟩ | rfl) <;> [exact hk; exact hiT]
      · intro hk
        by_cases hki : k = i
        · exact Or.inr hki
        · exact Or.inl ⟨hki, hk⟩
  · refine ⟨coalitionExchange δ x i T 1, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · intro k
      by_cases hk : k ∈ T
      · have hmono := coalitionExchange_monomial (δ := δ) (x := x) (i := i) (T := T)
          (ε := 1) hk
        have hchamber := hx k (hTS hk)
        linarith
      · rw [coalitionExchange_eq_of_notMem hk]
    · intro k hk
      rw [Finset.erase_eq_of_notMem hiT] at hk
      exact coalitionExchange_eq_of_notMem hk
    · exact decisiveSet_coalitionExchange hS δ hx hTS hT one_pos

/-- **The exchange distance.**  From a profile in the open chamber of `i`, the
minimal number of voters whose scores must be lowered in order to reach the cell
labelled `T` is exactly `|T \ {i}|`.  (`IsLeast`: the value is attained *and* is
a lower bound.) -/
theorem exchange_distance [DecidableEq ι] {S : Finset ι} (hS : S.Nonempty) (δ : ι → ℝ)
    {x : ι → ℝ} {i : ι} {T : Finset ι} (hxi : decisiveSet S hS δ x = {i})
    (hTS : T ⊆ S) (hT : T.Nonempty) :
    IsLeast {n : ℕ | ∃ (D : Finset ι) (y : ι → ℝ), D.card = n ∧ (∀ k, y k ≤ x k) ∧
      (∀ k ∉ D, y k = x k) ∧ decisiveSet S hS δ y = T} (T.erase i).card := by
  classical
  constructor
  · obtain ⟨y, hle, hoff, hy⟩ := exchange_upper_bound hS δ hxi hTS hT
    exact ⟨T.erase i, y, rfl, hle, hoff, hy⟩
  · rintro n ⟨D, y, rfl, hle, hoff, hy⟩
    exact Finset.card_le_card (exchange_lower_bound hS δ hxi hle hoff hy)

/-- **Exchange distance equals codimension.**  If the cell `T` is a face of the
chamber of the incumbent `i` (that is, `i ∈ T`), the exchange distance to it is
`|T| - 1`, which by `finrank_cellDirection` is exactly the codimension of the
cell in profile space. -/
theorem exchange_distance_eq_codim [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] {S : Finset ι} (hS : S.Nonempty)
    (δ : ι → ℝ) {x : ι → ℝ} {i : ι} {T : Finset ι} (hxi : decisiveSet S hS δ x = {i})
    (hTS : T ⊆ S) (hiT : i ∈ T) :
    IsLeast {n : ℕ | ∃ (D : Finset ι) (y : ι → ℝ), D.card = n ∧ (∀ k, y k ≤ x k) ∧
      (∀ k ∉ D, y k = x k) ∧ decisiveSet S hS δ y = T}
      (Fintype.card ι - Module.finrank ℝ (cellDirection (ι := ι) T)) := by
  classical
  have hT : T.Nonempty := ⟨i, hiT⟩
  have hrank := finrank_cellDirection (ι := ι) (T := T) hT
  ha
```

```
# Future directions: the single-voter exchange law and its geometry

Three research cycles were run on the tropical/social-choice chamber complex of
a min-plus aggregator `F x = min_{i ∈ S} (x i + δ i)`.

**Cycle 1 (sharpness).**  The catalog's one-directional exchange theorems
(`exchange_mem_wall`, `single_voter_exchange`) were upgraded to a *trichotomy
with no slack*: relative to the exchange threshold `θ = x i + δ i − δ j`, the
updated profile lies in the open cell `{j}` iff `c < θ`, on the wall `{i,j}` iff
`c = θ`, and in the incumbent's chamber iff `c ≥ θ`.  The master formula
`F(update x j c) = min (c + δ j) (x i + δ i)` makes the social score along the
exchange an explicit piecewise-affine function with a single kink at the wall.
A converse was proved: a downward single-voter move from chamber `{i}` into
chamber `{j}` must be a move of `j` itself.

**Cycle 2 (metric and combinatorics).**  The exchange law was made into a metric:
the minimum number of voters that must lower their scores in order to reach the
cell labelled `T` from the open chamber of `i` is *exactly* `|T \ {i}|`
(`IsLeast`), which for faces of that chamber equals the codimension
`n − dim(cellDirection T)`.  The dual graph of chambers is the complete graph;
the complex has `2^{|S|} − 1` cells with `f`-vector `choose |S| (d+1)` and Euler
characteristic `1`.  A proved counterexample shows the metric lower bound fails
for upward moves.

**Cycle 3 (rigidity).**  The aggregator as a function determines `(S, δ)`
exactly; the cell labelling alone determines `S` exactly and `δ` exactly up to a
single additive constant, and no further — an exact gauge statement.

The following conjectures are the natural next targets.

---

## 1. Exchange-metric realization of arbitrary polyhedral fans

**The key insight is** that the exchange distance `|T \ {i}|` is a purely
combinatorial quantity that computes a geometric codimension, so it should be a
*complete* invariant of the normal fan of a simplex, and fail to extend to
normal fans of general polytopes.

**Conjecture.**  A complete polyhedral fan in `ℝⁿ/ℝ·1` arises as the chamber
complex of some min-plus aggregator if and only if it is the normal fan of a
simplex; equivalently, iff its dual graph is complete and its `f`-vector is
`(choose n (d+1))_d`.

**Why now?**  Cycle 2 supplies both invariants (complete dual graph, binomial
`f`-vector) in verified Lean form, and cycle 3 supplies the rigidity needed to
```
